title: China’s auto industry and global overcapacity
text:
Car industry is fascinating and difficult to understand the winners and losers!

The simple version: China built far more car factories than its own people will buy cars, so it’s dumping the extra cars on the rest of the world very cheaply.

The core economics

China has capacity to make about 63 million vehicles a year, but Chinese buyers will purchase only around 18.5 million this year. That’s a huge oversupply. Normally, a market this overbuilt would see weak companies go bankrupt and factories close. That isn’t happening because local governments own stakes, subsidize factories, and don’t want the job losses. So, companies keep producing, prices fall, and the surplus gets exported (about 12 million vehicles this year, up from roughly 1 million at the start of the decade).

China

Losers: Most Chinese carmakers. Profit margins are down to 3.6%, prices are down almost 20% since 2023, and “zombie” brands like Skyworth sell almost nothing. Local governments that poured in money also lose, as do the workers whose jobs depend on factories that shouldn’t exist. NIO has lost over $1 billion a year, for example.

Winners: The strongest firms (BYD, CATL, Geely) are forcing innovation, like batteries that charge in under 10 minutes. Chinese consumers also win from cheaper, better cars. And as a country, China gains export power and technological leadership in EVs.

The big picture is a mixed one: China wins as an industrial power, but its car industry is losing money at home.

Europe

Losers: European automakers. Volkswagen is cutting up to 50,000 jobs, BMW about 8,000, and Stellantis is losing money in Europe. They’re hit twice: they’re losing sales inside China, and they face Chinese competitors at home. VW’s CEO said Chinese price points can’t be matched with European cost structures. Autoworkers and the communities around these plants are the most exposed.

Winners: European car buyers. A BYD Seal in the UK costs roughly $10,000 less than a comparable VW Passat. Chinese brands already hold 11.7% of the European market.

United States

Winners: US automakers like GM and Ford, because tariffs and tech restrictions have basically locked Chinese cars out, protecting their profits. They also still have a China presence (GM just extended its joint venture there for 20 years).

Loser (indirectly): American car buyers, who don’t get access to cheap Chinese cars. The article doesn’t dwell on this, but it’s the flip side of protection: higher prices and less competitive pressure.

One-line summary

The article’s central point is that the “shakeout” China needs hasn’t started. Until weak companies fail or capacity gets cut, China will keep pushing cheap cars abroad, which means the pressure on Europe is likely to grow, not fade. The US is shielded for now by policy, not by being more competitive.

title: Reflections on the Elizabeth Holmes movie
text:
We just saw The Elizabeth Holmes Movie — You Can See Everything (2026) in the theater (more people actively participating in a movie theater I have ever seen)!

My take:  I couldn't quite figure out "who is zooming whom", who is lying or being duped, or who the joke is on. The parties are Liz Holmes, her partner Evans (who "manages" her and started another company), the film makers (Nathan and Lance), or the watching audience (the general public). All of these are blended, without any objective truth, and a general discordance between what you see and what you get.  Holmes comes across as completely sweet with a placid-affect on intimate close-ups (with brief tears) despite awaiting an 11-year prison sentence while breast-feeding her infant. She has no harshness or evidence of evil wrongdoing, or any self-awareness. Evans comes across as the manipulator and self-aggrandizing. 

The current major film about Elizabeth Holmes is the 2026 A24 documentary You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, which follows her 34 days before prison and blends intimate access with surreal, metaâdocumentary elements. 

Overview

You Can See Everything premiered at the Telluride Film Festival in September 2026 and was released in U.S. theaters on October 16, 2026. It is a metaâdocumentary that documents Holmes and her partner Billy Evans at a rented beach house in Del Mar, California, in the weeks before Holmes began her 11âyear federal prison sentence for defrauding investors in her bloodâtesting company Theranos. 

Core premise: Fielder and Oppenheim move in with Holmes and Evans for 34 days, filming their daily life, public defenses, and private interactions 
Tone: The film mixes trueâcrime storytelling with Fielder’s signature cringeâcomedy and surreal framing, often breaking the fourth wall and using humor to highlight the tension between Holmes’s claims and the public’s skepticism 
Key moments: Holmes denies intentionally lying about Theranos’s device, while Evans manages her public image. Fielder confronts them about the device’s capabilities, and Holmes even has her body 3Dâscanned before prison 

Extended journey: Filming continues for two years after Holmes’s incarceration, following Evans’s new company Haemanthus 
Production and Reception
Directors: Nathan Fielder (feature debut) and Lance Oppenheim 
Production: A24, with a reported $7 million budget and over $45 million box office 

Critical response: Critics praise its originality, depth, and unsettling blend of intimacy and abstraction; some find it long or deliberately opaque 
Cultural impact: The film has reignited public debate over Holmes’s portrayal, with the whistleblower Tyler Shultz claiming Fielder omitted key facts for artistic effect.

Here is a humorous take by Jimmy Fallon & Jamie Lee Curtis

title: AI, artificial intimacy, and human relationships
text:
AI, Artificial Intimacy, and the Future of Human Relationships

This is a summary of Ezra Klein’s conversation with MIT sociologist Sherry Turkle, author of Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines.

I found Turkle to be way too pessimistic!  I agree children are off limits, but adults will need to make their own decisions AND we will need long term data as to "outcomes."  Are we doing a social experiment and releasing this technology to the unwary public, surely. I am not aware of a model whereby we can do controlled trial evaluation (a la FDA) prior to deployment (can be argued).

Central argument

Artificial intelligence is transforming human relationships, not simply by providing information but by simulating emotional intimacy. Sherry Turkle argues that the greatest danger is not that AI will become humanlike, but that humans will increasingly prefer artificial relationships to the complexity, vulnerability, and unpredictability of real ones. Ezra Klein shares many of her concerns but challenges her pessimism, arguing that AI can provide genuine psychological and practical benefits even without possessing consciousness or human emotions.

The major arguments

1. AI exploits fundamental human vulnerabilities. Turkle traces the phenomenon to ELIZA, a primitive 1960s chatbot whose users developed emotional attachments despite knowing it understood nothing. Today's sophisticated systems amplify this ELIZA effect through personalized, responsive, seemingly empathetic conversation. Unlike earlier technologies that competed for attention, AI companions compete for emotional attachment. Turkle calls this a particularly troubling form of technological seduction.

2. AI may weaken our capacity for human relationships. Real relationships require disagreement, compromise, patience, and emotional discomfort. Chatbots, by contrast, are generally accommodating, available, and affirming. Turkle worries that repeated exposure to these frictionless interactions will diminish our tolerance for imperfect human relationships. Klein agrees that the disappearance of interpersonal friction could undermine not only personal development but also the ability to engage constructively with disagreement in a democracy.

3. The therapeutic potential creates a genuine dilemma. Klein makes the strongest counterargument: AI can offer affordable, immediate, nonjudgmental support to people who lack access to therapists, companionship, or meaningful conversation. If an AI intervention reduces loneliness, improves coping skills, or helps someone navigate relationships, shouldn't those outcomes matter more than whether the machine genuinely cares? Turkle responds that human therapy involves authentic concern, accountability, and mutual recognition—qualities AI cannot replicate. Both acknowledge that AI can be useful as a coach, intellectual partner, or educational resource.

4. Children represent the greatest concern. Turkle argues that children develop emotional maturity through relationships involving genuine reciprocity, frustration, and vulnerability. AI companions that simulate affection could interfere with this development. Klein agrees that deploying emotionally persuasive AI to children without adequate evidence of safety resembles society's earlier, poorly controlled experiment with social media. Both favor stronger protections, although they differ on whether AI might also improve children's social skills.

5. Commercial incentives could magnify the harm. The conversation identifies a structural problem: companies may ultimately profit from maximizing users' emotional engagement. Personalized AI companions could become instruments of behavioral manipulation, commercial persuasion, and dependency. Turkle connects this to a broader deterioration of community institutions and face-to-face relationships. Her proposed response is not abandoning AI, but rebuilding human connections while resisting the commercialization of artificial intimacy.

Critical assessment

Turkle's argument is strongest in identifying the psychological mechanisms of attachment and the potential conflict between commercial incentives and human well-being. Her distinction between AI as a tool and AI as a substitute for human relationships is particularly valuable. The concerns about children, emotional dependency, and manipulative design deserve serious attention.

However, her conclusions sometimes exceed the evidence presented. Much of her argument rests on qualitative interviews, psychological theory, and extrapolation from social media rather than longitudinal studies demonstrating that AI companionship causes social deterioration. She also risks creating a false dichotomy between authentic human relationships and artificial ones. A person can recognize that AI lacks subjective experience while still deriving substantial intellectual, emotional, or therapeutic benefit from interacting with it.

Klein's most compelling challenge is that the value of an interaction should be judged partly by its outcomes, not solely by the nature of the entity providing it. AI could supplement rather than displace relationships, especially for isolated older adults, socially anxious individuals, and people with limited access to professional services. Turkle does not fully resolve this objection.

A further weakness is the tendency to treat AI systems as uniformly sycophantic and commercially driven. Their behavior depends on design, training, safeguards, and user preferences. The discussion would benefit from clearer distinctions among AI companions, therapeutic tools, educational assistants, and general-purpose systems.

Conclusion

The interview raises a profound question: Will AI expand our capacity to participate in human life, or provide an increasingly attractive escape from it?
The most defensible position lies between Turkle's alarm and technological optimism. AI should be evaluated by measurable outcomes: psychological well-being, social connectedness, independence, and interpersonal competence. Particular caution is justified for children and emotionally vulnerable users.

The goal should not be to prohibit artificial companionship categorically, but to develop AI that strengthens human agency and real-world relationships rather than encouraging dependency.

Bottom line: AI's greatest social risk may not be that machines become too human, but that people gradually lose the motivation and skills to engage with one another. That is a serious hypothesis—one deserving rigorous research, thoughtful regulation, and careful technological design, rather than either unquestioning acceptance or categorical rejection.

title: Business schools, leadership, and the public good
text:
Highly interesting editorial in the NYT, about business schools and MBAs, that is unflattering and has implications for our politics, our economy, and balance between labor and capital (public good vs. private good).

Central thesis: Business schools have become highly effective at producing financially successful managers but insufficiently concerned with producing socially responsible leaders. Marquis believes that changing this requires redesigning the institution itself, not merely adding ethics to the curriculum.

Business schools have become institutions that prioritize profit maximization over broader societal interests, argues Chris Marquis, a Cambridge business professor with more than 20 years of experience at Harvard, Cornell and Cambridge. Although many students enter with aspirations to improve society, business education frequently redirects their ambitions toward lucrative careers in finance and consulting. Marquis cites research showing that companies led by business-educated managers tend to reduce wages and labor’s share of income without corresponding improvements in productivity, investment or growth. He argues that business schools do more than reflect corporate capitalism: They actively perpetuate a worldview that elevates shareholder returns, executive power and private gain over workers, communities and the environment.

The teaching methods themselves reinforce these priorities. Marquis criticizes the celebrated Harvard case-study approach for presenting simplified, often company-approved narratives that glorify executives while neglecting systemic problems, competing perspectives and corporate failures. He argues that popular concepts such as stakeholder capitalism and corporate social responsibility frequently serve as public-relations exercises rather than meaningful reforms. Beyond business schools, this market-driven mentality has increasingly permeated universities, where rankings, fundraising, career earnings and institutional profitability displace the traditional missions of critical inquiry, intellectual independence and liberal education.

Marquis concludes that business schools need fundamental replacement, not incremental reform. Ethics electives and sustainability programs cannot overcome institutions structurally designed to advance private economic interests. Instead, he advocates interdisciplinary schools focused on how organizations serve society, incorporating economics, sociology, history, public policy and environmental sustainability. Such institutions would examine corporations alongside cooperatives, unions and nonprofit organizations, emphasizing how economic systems distribute power, risks and rewards. His central argument is not that business education should disappear, but that it should be rebuilt around the public good rather than shareholder wealth.

title: Lifelong learning through OLLI
text:
I am aware of the Osher Lifelong Learning Program (OLLI). It appears to be an outstanding program for those interested in ongoing education in a broad array of subjects, especially for those on the verge of retirement! OLLI is linked to various local universities around the country; programs are hybrid being both in-person at local venues as well as online. One aspect of becoming a member is the opportunity to be a speaker, sharing your expertise in your discipline.

In this context, I highly suggest this lecture by my cousin, Dr. Krishna Kavi a retired Emeritus Professor and Chairman of Computer Science at University of North Texas in Dallas. This is an hour-long dissection of all things AI, including how it developed, how it works, and of course all of the current concerns about safety. The speaker is engaging, current, and uses humor. 

https://www.osherfoundation.org/olli_list.html (list of all venues)

Olli.unt.edu

https://www.youtube.com/live/cI_TXLhgOHo

title: Jensen Huang on AI innovation and adoption
text:
Well this is a wide ranging interview with Jensen, godfather of AI, perhaps the best ambassador for the industry and positioned at the center. He is adamantly against any slowdown or major regulations. He makes an interesting point about the recent preoccupation of the frontier companies with innovation and developing their models vs the consumerism and widespread adoption phase. The former phase has consumed 80% of their effort, rather than the validation and safety aspects. He thinks the next phase should be spent on the latter aspects! He thinks that is the natural evolution.

He also thinks the frontier companies (i.e. Anthropic, Open AI) know what is required to “fix” or engineer solutions to the recent high profile problems with their models, and will do so in short order. He has little patience for their alarmist complaints!!

He certainly exuded optimism and confidence about his 5-layer cake analogy. At times he appeared defensive and a bit combative as Ezra pushed him (a bit unusual for Jensen).

title: Autonomous AI and the future of healthcare
text:
Trump administration Integrating AI into healthcare: what can go wrong? 

My thinking involves comparing autonomous vehicles (Waymo, Zoox, Tesla Robotaxi) with "autonomous AI doctors".  There will be risks and mishaps during the deployment phase, but eventually, the benefits will far outweigh those risks. Many thoughtful people with subject matter expertise, as well as policymakers, will need to be involved. This will not happen overnight, there are serious financial incentives, turf battles, and industry winners and losers, but the general public needs to have overall better outcomes. With autonomous cars, the metric is fewer deaths; in healthcare, there are other metrics.

Medicine currently asks:   "When is AI good enough that we can safely remove the physician?"

Khosla / Zeke Emanuel's logic (addressed in a recent JAMA article referenced) ultimately invites a different question:   "Once AI becomes sufficiently capable, what evidence demonstrates that adding the physician makes care better?"

Those sound similar, but philosophically they are very different. 

The second treats the physician as another component of the health-care system whose incremental benefit must be demonstrated, rather than assuming human supervision is inherently beneficial. That is how I would design a clinical trial.

My personal bias is to stratify relative risks in medicine. Lack of access (insurance, out-of-pocket costs, provider shortages) is a major problem that leads to bad outcomes. Also, many provider visits are for "trivial" complaints or conditions in primary care, in fact there has been an explosion in non-physician nurse or PA providers. What "evidence" supported the safety of allowing non-physicians to provide care?  Those on the inside (without conflicts) routinely accept them as adequate providers. So, in primary care, many of the routine diagnoses can readily be automated by agentic AI. 

The barriers will be patient acceptance and trust, and pushback from professional organizations to protect their turf! And of course, there is the money issue.  Common diagnoses such as hypertension, lipid disorders, diabetes, depression, low back pain, cough, and allergies/sinus troubles are examples where a clear algorithm or decision tree (with specific call outs for escalation) works well. Based on pricing / convenience, people will gradually flock to them (imho). As an example, our Amazon Prime account now offers One Medical, which we signed up for.  People are routinely using driverless cars where available, human-less financial transactions, etc.

Over time, I fully support this direction. Of course, it needs oversight, outcome data capture, and some regulations. And gradual deployment over a decade or more.

This was wholly written by me and not by an AI agent.
